seeds.title: Digital root of n equals n reduced mod 9 (9 for nonzero multiples of 9)
seeds.statement: For n >= 1 the base-10 digital root dr(n) — the iterated digit sum taken until a single digit remains — equals 1 + ((n - 1) mod 9); equivalently dr(n) = n mod 9 except that dr(n) = 9 whenever 9 | n and n != 0. This is a theorem, not an empirical pattern: it follows immediately from 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9). It is the fact the whole '3-6-9' folklore is built on.
seeds.source_citation: Weisstein, 'Digital Root', Wolfram MathWorld; OEIS A010888 (digital root of n)
seeds.author: OEIS/MathWorld

verification.method: OEIS A010888 definition confirmed verbatim (a(n) = n mod 9, 0->9; if the initial 0 is ignored the sequence is periodic with period 9); MathWorld 'Digital Root' cross-check; proved directly from 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9); Python-checked dr(n) == (9 if 9|n else n%9) for n = 1..999 (all True).

seeds.title: n ≡ digit-sum(n) (mod 9) — the base-10 / mod-9 congruence
seeds.statement: Every base-10 integer is congruent mod 9 to the sum of its digits, because 10^k ≡ 1 (mod 9) for every k >= 0. This is the lemma underneath the entire digital-root / casting-out-nines apparatus, and the concrete reason the modulus is 9 (namely 9 = 10 - 1) rather than any mystical property of the number.
seeds.source_citation: G. H. Hardy & E. M. Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers (6th ed., OUP 2008), congruences chapter; Weisstein, 'Casting Out Nines', Wolfram MathWorld
seeds.author: Hardy & Wright / MathWorld

verification.method: Standard number theory: 10^k ≡ 1 (mod 9) => n = sum(d_k 10^k) ≡ sum(d_k) (mod 9). Cross-checked against MathWorld 'Casting Out Nines'.

seeds.title: Digital root is a mod-9 homomorphism (casting out nines)
seeds.statement: The digital root respects addition and multiplication: dr(a + b) = dr(dr(a) + dr(b)) and dr(a·b) = dr(dr(a)·dr(b)), because reduction mod 9 is a ring homomorphism Z -> Z/9Z. This is the classical 'casting out nines' arithmetic check. Note its honest limit: it can reveal an error but never certify correctness — any mistake that is a multiple of 9 passes undetected.
seeds.author: MathWorld

verification.method: Follows from Z/9Z being a ring: reduction mod 9 is a homomorphism, and dr is that reduction with 0 renamed 9 on nonzero multiples of 9. MathWorld 'Casting Out Nines' confirms statement and the multiple-of-9 blind spot.

seeds.title: The digital-root sequence is purely periodic with period 9
seeds.statement: The sequence dr(1), dr(2), dr(3), ... = 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,1,2,3,... is purely periodic with period exactly 9 (OEIS A010888, ignoring the a(0) = 0 term). This is the 'the number line wraps onto a 9-cycle' fact that the 3-6-9 wheel diagrams visualise — a periodicity of the counting numbers mod 9, nothing more.
seeds.canonical_statement: dr(n + 9) = dr(n) for all n >= 1; fundamental period = 9
seeds.source_citation: OEIS A010888 (digital root of n): 'If the initial 0 term is ignored, the sequence is periodic with period 9.'
seeds.author: OEIS

verification.method: OEIS A010888 comment confirmed verbatim in web check; immediate corollary of dr(n) = 1 + ((n-1) mod 9).

seeds.title: The doubling orbit mod 9 is 1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8 -> 7 -> 5 -> 1 (period 6)
seeds.statement: Repeated doubling of digital roots cycles 1,2,4,8,7,5 and back with period exactly 6: dr(2^k) for k >= 0 is 1,2,4,8,7,5,1,2,4,... The period is 6 because the multiplicative order of 2 modulo 9 is 6. Crucially, the residues 3, 6 and 9 NEVER appear in this orbit — that exclusion is the exact, provable content of the vortex 'family-number' split, and it is elementary group theory.
seeds.source_citation: OEIS A000079 (powers of 2) reduced mod 9; the multiplicative order of 2 mod 9 is 6 (standard; cf. Weisstein, 'Multiplicative Order', Wolfram MathWorld)
seeds.author: OEIS / MathWorld

verification.method: Python-computed 2^k mod 9 for k = 0..11 = [1,2,4,8,7,5,1,2,4,8,7,5]; multiplicative order of 2 mod 9 computed = 6. Residues 3,6,9 absent by inspection.

seeds.title: (Z/9Z)* is cyclic of order 6; 2 and 5 are primitive roots
seeds.statement: The multiplicative group of units mod 9 is {1,2,4,5,7,8}, cyclic of order phi(9) = 6, generated by 2 (and by 5). Every unit's order divides 6: ord(1)=1, ord(8)=2, ord(4)=3, ord(7)=3, ord(2)=6, ord(5)=6. This is why every digital-root multiplicative orbit (doubling, tripling of units, etc.) closes within at most 6 steps — a theorem of Gauss (units mod an odd prime power are cyclic), not numerology.
seeds.source_citation: C. F. Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801) — (Z/p^k Z)* is cyclic for odd primes p; Weisstein, 'Modulo Multiplication Group' & 'Primitive Root', Wolfram MathWorld
seeds.author: Gauss / MathWorld

verification.method: Python-computed units mod 9 = {1,2,4,5,7,8} and orders {1:1,2:6,4:3,5:6,7:3,8:2}; group order = phi(9) = 6; elements of order 6 (primitive roots) = {2,5}. Cyclicity is Gauss's classical theorem.

seeds.title: Under doubling mod 9, {3,6} is a 2-cycle and 9 is fixed
seeds.statement: The non-unit residues behave as their own closed system: doubling swaps 3 and 6 (a 2-cycle: 2·3 = 6, 2·6 = 12 ≡ 3) and fixes 9 (2·9 = 18 ≡ 9, i.e. 0 mod 9). So 3, 6 and 9 form a closed orbit-set disjoint from the 1-2-4-8-7-5 unit orbit. This closure is precisely what Rodin's 'doubling circuit' diagram draws — the arithmetic is classical and provable; any significance beyond the arithmetic is a separate, non-established claim (see rodin-vortex-energy-leap).
seeds.source_citation: Elementary mod-9 arithmetic; this is the kernel of Rodin's 'Mathematical Fingerprint of God' doubling map (see rodin-doubling-kernel-classical)
seeds.author: elementary

verification.method: Python-computed (3*2)%9 = 6, (6*2)%9 = 3, (9*2)%9 = 0 (≡ 9). Closure of {3,6,9} under doubling by direct check.

seeds.title: 3, 6, 9 are exactly the digital roots not coprime to 9
seeds.statement: Among digital roots 1..9, exactly {3,6,9} share a factor with 9 (they are the multiples of 3); the other six {1,2,4,5,7,8} are the units mod 9. This is the precise, checkable reason 3-6-9 stand apart: they are the non-units — the ideal 3Z/9Z = {0,3,6} together with 9 ≡ 0 — not the units that generate the doubling circuit. Multiplying ANY digital root by 3 lands inside {3,6,9}; the set is an absorbing multiplicative sink, which is a fact of ring structure, not a message about the cosmos.
seeds.source_citation: Elementary ideal/coset structure of Z/9Z (the ideal 3Z/9Z = {0,3,6}); standard, cf. Hardy & Wright (2008)
seeds.author: elementary

verification.method: gcd(k,9) > 1 iff 3 | k for k in 1..9, giving {3,6,9}; complement {1,2,4,5,7,8} = units (matches units-mod-9-cyclic-order-6). 3·x mod 9 ∈ {0,3,6} for all x, verified by direct computation.

seeds.title: Digital roots of squares cycle 1,4,9,7,7,9,4,1,9 (period 9)
seeds.statement: dr(n^2) is periodic with period 9: 1,4,9,7,7,9,4,1,9 repeating. The values are confined to {1,4,7,9} because the quadratic residues mod 9 are exactly {0,1,4,7}. A provable consequence of squaring being well-defined on Z/9Z (n^2 mod 9 depends only on n mod 9); any 'pattern' restating it is known mathematics, not a discovery.
seeds.canonical_statement: dr(n^2) has period 9 with value-set {1,4,7,9}; QR mod 9 = {0,1,4,7}
seeds.source_citation: Quadratic residues mod 9 = {0,1,4,7} (standard); digital roots of n^2 by direct reduction (n^2 mod 9 depends only on n mod 9)
seeds.author: elementary

seeds.title: Fibonacci numbers mod 9 are periodic with Pisano period pi(9) = 24
seeds.statement: The Fibonacci sequence reduced mod 9 repeats with period exactly 24 — the Pisano period pi(9). OEIS A001175 (Pisano periods) has a(9) = 24. Because reduction mod 9 and the digital-root map agree up to renaming 0 as 9, the digital roots of the Fibonacci numbers inherit this period-24 structure.
seeds.source_citation: OEIS A001175 (Pisano periods), a(9) = 24; Weisstein, 'Pisano Period', Wolfram MathWorld
seeds.author: OEIS / MathWorld

verification.method: Python-computed Pisano period of Fibonacci mod 9 = 24 (first return of the pair (F_k, F_{k+1}) to (0,1)); matches OEIS A001175 term a(9) = 24 confirmed by web check.

seeds.title: Digital roots of Fibonacci numbers: the 24-term cycle
seeds.statement: dr(F_n) is periodic with period 24: 1,1,2,3,5,8,4,3,7,1,8,9,8,8,7,6,4,1,5,6,2,8,1,9 (OEIS A030132). Real, checkable structure the '24-cycle' folklore points at: positions 12 and 24 are both 9, and for the other eleven positions dr(F_k) + dr(F_{k+12}) = 9. It is a corollary of the Pisano period pi(9) = 24 (see fibonacci-pisano-period-9), not evidence of anything beyond mod-9 arithmetic.
seeds.author: OEIS

verification.method: Python-computed dr(F_n) for n = 1..48: first 24 terms = [1,1,2,3,5,8,4,3,7,1,8,9,8,8,7,6,4,1,5,6,2,8,1,9] and terms 25..48 identical (period 24 confirmed). 9-complement structure (dr(F_k)+dr(F_{k+12}) = 9 except the two 9s at positions 12,24) checked by hand against the cycle. Cycle matches OEIS A030132 verbatim (web-confirmed).

seeds.title: Lucas numbers mod 9 also have period 24
seeds.statement: The Lucas sequence (L_0 = 2, L_1 = 1) reduced mod 9 is periodic with period 24 — the same as the Fibonacci Pisano period, because any sequence obeying the Fibonacci recurrence mod m has period dividing pi(m). So the celebrated digital-root '24-cycle' is a property of the recurrence mod 9, not something unique to the Fibonacci numbers — a useful de-mystifier.
seeds.source_citation: Standard Pisano-period theory: the period of any second-order Fibonacci-type recurrence mod m divides pi(m); pi(9) = 24 (OEIS A001175). Lucas period mod 9 verified by direct computation.
seeds.author: elementary / OEIS

verification.method: Python-computed period of Lucas sequence mod 9 (first return of (L_k, L_{k+1}) to (2,1)) = 24; divides pi(9) = 24 as the theory predicts.

seeds.title: Digital roots of triangular numbers cycle 1,3,6,1,6,3,1,9,9 (period 9)
seeds.statement: For triangular numbers T_n = n(n+1)/2, dr(T_n) is periodic with period 9: 1,3,6,1,6,3,1,9,9 repeating. The values are drawn from {1,3,6,9} and every third term is a multiple of 3. Provable because T_{n+9} - T_n = 9(n+5), so T_n mod 9 depends only on n mod 9 — a figurate-number fact, checkable to any N.
seeds.source_citation: Triangular numbers OEIS A000217; digital-root reduction with the identity T_{n+9} - T_n = 9(n+5) (verified by direct computation)
seeds.author: elementary / OEIS

It does not appear in Tesla's published writings, patents, correspondence, or contemporaneous biographies; the earliest online traces date to around 2013, and it is catalogued among misattributed/unsourced quotations.
